events.text:
⚡🇪🇺🛢️ IEA: Diesel Markets to Stay Tight Well Into 2027
The International Energy Agency warned that global diesel supplies are likely to remain constrained well into 2027. The main causes are the Iran war's disruption of Middle East refining and exports and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries. In its monthly Oil Market Report, the agency said combined net gasoil/diesel exports from the Middle East and Russia fell by 1.3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, to 820,000 b/d in September. Higher shipments from the US and China only partly offset the loss. European diesel refining margins hit a record of almost $95 a barrel in September. Wholesale diesel prices topped $200 a barrel. The IEA expects refinery output to recover and return to a seasonal surplus in early 2027, but says rebuilding depleted inventories is unlikely before the second half of 2027. G7 leaders pledged on 2 October to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks over four months. That pledge largely accelerates delivery of an IEA release agreed in March rather than adding new barrels. The IEA warned that oil markets "may experience more turmoil in the months ahead."

💵 Hormuz’s costly aftershock: Why fuel crisis may outlast the US’ Iran war gamble 
[Recovering crude exports](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75852) from the Persian Gulf have [done little to ease the fuel squeeze.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75920)
Non-Iranian Gulf crude exports reached at least 16.5 million barrels per day in September, matching pre-war levels (Kpler), yet damaged refining capacity, depleted inventories and soaring shipping costs keep[ diesel prices](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74676) elevated.
♦️ Gulf diesel and gasoil exports averaged 390,000 barrels per day in August - over a quarter of pre-war levels (IEA)
♦️ longer routes, ship-to-ship transfers and alternative pipelines consume tanker capacity, lift freight rates and raise delivered fuel costs
♦️ Saudi Arabia’s East–West Pipeline pumping stations and Red Sea export terminals remain vulnerable to [Houthi strikes ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76201)
♦️ [energy trade is risky & costly](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76051): by early October, tanker captains could earn up to $100,000 a month, while[ war-risk insurance for Hormuz crossings](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75852) reached 6–10% of hull value (~ $20 million for supertanker)
As a result, diesel and jet fuel prices have surged: US diesel averaged $6.20 per gallon on October 5 (nearly 63% above its late-February level), while Brent crude rose around 45%.
Restoring crude flows is not the same as restoring the fuel market, and even after regional escalation subsides, repairs, refinery restarts and sustained shipping security will require time.

🇨🇳🇮🇱China turns civilian flight data into tool for tracking Israeli electronic warfare
Chinese military researchers have developed a low-cost method to pinpoint suspected electronic warfare units without resorting to specialized surveillance equipment, reports SCMP.
♦️ a team from the PLA’s Information Engineering University analyzed 43 days of civil aviation data from February 27 to April 10 - covering the period surrounding the US-Israeli war unleashed on Iran.
♦️ GPS spoofing manipulates navigation signals to make aircraft or drones report false positions – yet its effects can show up in flight-tracking records as sudden jumps that defy normal flight patterns
♦️ an algorithm was used to filter out anomalies and estimate where the interference originated
♦️ two suspected sources in the Mediterranean near Israel were identified with estimated positioning errors of 10.9–18.9 km
♦️ one area was roughly 80 km northwest of Haifa; another was about 30 km northwest of the Gaza Strip
The researchers assessed that the first source may have been countering long-range Iranian Shahed-136 drones, requiring sophisticated, dynamic spoofing. 
👉 The second may have targeted shorter-range drones like those reportedly used by Palestinian armed groups and Yemen’s Houthi movement.
The researchers claim future work could incorporate ship-navigation data, potentially expanding the method’s reach across maritime environments.

🪖 Ukrainian commanders compare Starlink slowdown to ‘nuclear strike’
“This is comparable to a nuclear strike against us. All operations are on hold. This will cost many of our lives,” a Ukrainian officer told Politico, commenting on the [restrictions](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76194) Ukraine’s drone operators are experiencing using Elon Musk’s satellite internet tech.
The officer said “all Starlink and Starshield terminals” used by Ukraine have been hit with a 100 km/h speed limit, confirming that the slowdown was deliberate.
💬 “We can no longer fight effectively to support our infantry on the battlefield. We can no longer strike multiple-launch rocket systems, North Korean-supplied heavy self-propelled artillery positioned deep behind enemy lines, ammunition depots, command centers and other targets,” they added, failing to mention the strikes which also regularly target civilians.
A Ukrainian defense ministry official said the speed cap ranges from 72-161 km/h, “depending on the specific vehicle and unit.” At these speeds, it’s much easier for Russia’s multilayered air defense network to engage them.
👉 European officials slammed SpaceX over the “politicized” move, with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asking “big man” Elon Musk whether he was “playing politics with [his] products again,” and warning that “European customers…are watching.”
Musk and SpaceX have yet to comment on the speed cap. Last week, Musk said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new leader” while reacting to Trump’s criticism of Zelensky for continuing strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and raising global diesel prices.

🇺🇸💸 $12 BILLION, three years late — US still can’t fully field its first hypersonic missile
The US Army’s Dark Eagle is now more than three years behind schedule and still has not been declared fully fielded after missing deadlines in 2023 and 2025, Bloomberg reported. The Pentagon has spent more than $12 billion on hypersonic programs since 2018, while Army officials have acknowledged “quality defects” on the Lockheed Martin production line. 
Meanwhile, Russia has been operating an entire family of hypersonic weapons for years:
🌏 Kinzhal — on experimental combat duty since December 2017, nearly nine years ago; Russia reports speeds of up to Mach 10 and a range exceeding 2,000 km.
🌏 Avangard — first regiment entered combat duty in December 2019. Russian officials have reported speeds of around Mach 27.
🌏 Zircon — deployed aboard the frigate Admiral Gorshkov in January 2023; Russian officials put its speed at Mach 9 and range at over 1,000 km.
So while Russia was already putting hypersonic systems on combat duty years ago, the US is still “continuing fielding activities” for its first one.
